items.text: Bahrain's military said it shot down several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they hit a U.S. base there.
items.detail: It was the first time since September that Bahraini air defenses had to intercept attacks; the Interior Ministry twice warned residents to take shelter. The Guards said they launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for "hostile U.S. actions," Iranian state media reported. There was no immediate comment from the U.S. military. Two days earlier the U.S. denied an Iranian claim of hitting a radar in Bahrain, saying it intercepted two drones without damage. Separately, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said they were pulling back from the area overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, leaving the Houthis in control of it.
items.why: Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and new attacks there strain a fragile lull in the Iran war.

items.text: A Copa Airlines jet and a UPS cargo plane collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries.
items.detail: The FAA said the wingtip of the Copa Boeing 737, which had just landed from Panama City, struck the nose of the UPS Boeing 767 around 9:15 p.m.; controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight. All 166 passengers and six crew members got off the Copa plane. The two injured people were treated at the scene. The FAA is investigating. It came a day after the nationwide ground stop.
items.why: It is another safety scare in a week of air travel disruption.

items.text: East Potomac Park and its public golf course in Washington can't be closed for now, a federal judge ruled Saturday, hours before Trump's planned shutdown.
items.detail: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order through Nov. 28 barring the government from closing the park and course during their usual hours; the course was due to close Sunday for a 15-month rebuild into a championship venue. She cited Trump's own social media posts on the closure date and said the government's reasons appeared to be after-the-fact justifications, but she did not order it to actively manage the park. The suit was brought by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers. Trump criticized the judge on social media Saturday.
items.why: It keeps a heavily used public park open while the court weighs Trump's redevelopment plan.

items.text: The tanker's voyage data recorder from Friday's New Orleans cruise ship collision has been recovered, the NTSB said, with a preliminary report due within 30 days.
items.detail: The recorder captures the ship's speed, direction and course plus audio from the bridge. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said 16 investigators are on site for about a week and plan interviews; a final report is expected in 18 to 24 months. The cause of the Atlantic Asphalt's apparent steering loss is still unknown. Mayor Helena Moreno said it could take weeks to remove the sunken American Heritage.
items.why: The data recorder is the key evidence for what made the tanker veer into the docked ship.

items.text: SpaceX's Starship upper stage was caught by its launch tower's arms Saturday, the first time a ship returning from orbit has been recovered that way.
items.detail: Ship 42 came back to Starbase, Texas, after about 14 orbits and nearly a day in space on Flight 15, which lifted off Friday and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites. SpaceX confirmed the catch at about 3:21 p.m. CT. The other half of the planned double recovery failed Friday: the Super Heavy booster aborted its own tower catch and was sent to a splashdown in the Gulf. SpaceX had caught boosters on three earlier flights but had never tried to catch the ship.
items.why: Catching the ship is a key step toward a fully reusable rocket, which SpaceX says is needed to cut launch costs and fly to the Moon and Mars.

items.text: Peoria's evacuation order was lifted Saturday after a search of the ethanol plant where a bomb was found turned up no other devices.
items.detail: Police Chief Brad Dixon ended the one-mile evacuation around Peoria's BioUrja Renewables plant at 1 p.m. CT, about a day after more than 5,000 people were told to leave; East Peoria's zone and the Illinois River also reopened. No arrests have been made, and officials would not discuss the device, suspects or a motive. The FBI and ATF are investigating.
items.why: The immediate danger is over, but whoever planted the bomb has not been found.

items.text: Friday's nationwide flight halt began during contractor L3Harris's routine swap of old FAA phone lines to fiber, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
items.detail: Duffy said the work at a remote FAA site flooded air traffic control routers with connection attempts; investigators are still checking whether it was installer error or a faulty router. L3Harris said it is cooperating. FAA chief Bryan Bedford said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or of an AI tool's role, expected 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations Saturday, and said airlines should be back on full schedules by Sunday night. Duffy raised his request to Congress for air traffic control upgrades to $50 billion.
items.why: The cause points to the aging system's fragility a week and a half before Thanksgiving travel, and sets up a funding fight in Congress.

items.text: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said U.S. negotiators asked for the first time whether Ukraine would leave the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.
items.detail: In remarks released by his office Saturday, Zelensky said Ukraine will not give up land but that he would put a full package, with security guarantees, a strong army and rebuilding funds, to a national referendum if the U.S. and NATO partners confirm it. He rejected Russia's call to settle European security first and dismissed Putin's offer of a local truce in Kostiantynivka. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met him in Dublin on Thursday after talks with Putin.
items.why: It is the first sign that NATO membership is on the table in U.S.-led talks to end the war.

items.text: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska's governor's race, the AP projected, the first Democrat elected to the office since 1998.
items.detail: The former state lawmaker defeated three Republicans, including Trump-endorsed Bernadette Wilson; AP called the race at 12:01 a.m. EST Saturday. He succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and was endorsed by Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski. His win means Democrats will hold 30 governorships. Alaska voters also rejected a ballot measure to repeal the state's open primaries and ranked-choice general elections.
items.why: It extends the Democrats' midterm sweep of state governments to a long-Republican state.

also.text: Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the United States after 26 years, health officials in the Americas decided, Reuters and others reported.
also.detail: An independent commission that reports to the Pan American Health Organization concluded at its Nov. 10-13 meeting that the same measles strain had spread in the U.S. for more than a year, according to Reuters (first reported by The Wall Street Journal), CNN and KFF Health News. PAHO plans to announce it Tuesday, Nov. 17. The CDC counted 5,412 confirmed cases this year through Nov. 12, more than double 2025's total, the most since the early 1990s. An outbreak in Utah passed one year in June. The U.S. had held elimination status since 2000; Canada lost it last year. An HHS spokesperson blamed vaccination gaps that opened before this administration. Wisconsin reported its second child death in its outbreak Friday.
also.why: The status loss means measles is spreading on its own in the U.S. again, putting babies too young for the vaccine and others at higher risk.

also.text: Workday's payroll and HR service was restored by 11 a.m. ET Saturday after Friday's outage, the company said.
also.detail: A Workday spokesperson said customers were coming back online and apologized. The company said the disruption began after a problem found while testing its backup systems left some data in an inconsistent state. Some employers warned updates between systems could lag while cleanup finishes.
also.why: Workers at thousands of employers can again reach timecards and pay information.

also.text: Bitcoin fell to about $65,000 Saturday, its lowest in three months, after losing about 13.5% over the past week.
also.detail: The largest cryptocurrency slid nearly 3% more after U.S. stock markets closed Friday. Over the week, ether fell 18%, XRP 16.3% and solana 18%, CoinDesk reported. Bitcoin traded above $80,000 in September.
also.why: The slide wipes out the fall rally for many recent buyers.

week.text: The FAA's nationwide ground stop ended at 8:15 p.m. Friday after more than four hours, and officials blamed overloaded, decades-old network equipment.
week.detail: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said radar and communications at air traffic control centers began showing "instability" shortly after 3:30 p.m. ET, and the FAA halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data ... and because of that, we shut the system down," he said at a White House briefing, blaming "an incredibly old air traffic control system" and asking Congress for billions to overhaul it. AP reported officials said new technology being added to the system overloaded the antiquated equipment, causing intermittent communications and radar gaps. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said nothing so far pointed to a cyberattack. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years; more than 2,000 flights were canceled Saturday, and Duffy said operations should be back to normal by Thanksgiving travel.
week.why: It stranded travelers nationwide and puts the aging air traffic system and its funding at the center of Congress's agenda.

week.text: All U.S. airports were ordered to stop departures Friday afternoon after a communications failure hit the FAA's air traffic control centers.
week.detail: The FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center ordered a national ground stop at 3:53 p.m. ET "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," telling all departing traffic to stay on the ground until further notice; inbound international flights are handled case by case and planes already in the air may land. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communication issue was affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers and FAA technicians were investigating. No cause or restart time had been given as of about 4:45 p.m. ET. The last nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, when a pilot-notice system failed.
week.why: A nationwide halt of departures strands travelers across the country on a Friday evening and raises questions about the air traffic system's reliability.
week.source: FAA Air Traffic Control System Command Center advisory

week.text: A river cruise ship with about 129 passengers rolled onto its side in New Orleans after a tanker struck it at the dock.
week.detail: The tanker Atlantic Asphalt hit American Cruise Lines' paddlewheeler American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. CT Friday on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans administration building, about two hours after it docked to let passengers off, the port said. Rescuers pulled people from the water; the mayor's office said about a dozen people were taken to hospitals and search-and-rescue work was continuing. The cruise line said guests and crew were evacuated. The Coast Guard closed the river between mile markers 93 and 96. Officials have not confirmed the number of injuries or the cause.
week.why: It is a major maritime accident on the nation's busiest commercial river, with many passengers aboard.
